<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">PART&nbsp;I<a name="Parti_072542"></a></font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Item
1.&#160; Business</font></u></b><a name="Item1_Business_072543"></a></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">General</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Alliance Bancorp,&nbsp;Inc.
of Pennsylvania (&#147;Alliance Bancorp&#148; or the &#147;Company&#148;) is a federally chartered
savings and loan holding company which owns 100% of the capital stock of
Alliance Bank (&#147;Bank&#148;), which is a Pennsylvania chartered community oriented
savings bank headquartered in Broomall, Pennsylvania.&#160; On January&nbsp;30, 2007, the Bank completed
a reorganization to a mid-tier holding company structure.&#160; In the reorganization and offering, the
Company sold 1,807,339 shares of common stock at a purchase price of $10.00 per
share and issued 5,417,661 shares of common stock in exchange for former
outstanding shares of Alliance Bank (the &#147;Bank&#148;).&#160; Each share of the Bank&#146;s common stock was
converted into 2.09945 shares of the Company&#146;s common stock.&#160; The offering resulted in approximately $16.5
million in net proceeds to the Company.&#160;
The significant asset of the Company is the capital stock of the Bank.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Alliance Bank operates a
total of nine banking offices located in Delaware and Chester Counties, which
are suburbs of Philadelphia.&#160; Our primary
business consists of attracting deposits from the general public and using
those funds, together with funds we borrow, to originate loans to our customers
and invest in securities such as U.S. Government and agency securities,
mortgage-backed securities and municipal obligations.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009, we had $464.2
million of total assets, $378.3 million of total deposits and stockholders&#146;
equity of $48.4 million.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company is
subject to supervision and regulation by the Office of Thrift Supervision (&#147;OTS&#148;).&#160; The Bank is subject to regulation by the
Pennsylvania Department of Banking (the &#147;Department&#148;), as its chartering
authority and primary regulator, and by the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (the &#147;FDIC&#148;), which insures the Bank&#146;s deposits up to applicable
limits.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Market Area and Competition</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Alliance Bank is headquartered in Broomall, Pennsylvania and conducts
its business through eight offices located in Delaware County, Pennsylvania,
and one office in Chester County, Pennsylvania.&#160;
The primary market areas served by Alliance Bank are Delaware and
Chester Counties, Philadelphia, and the suburban areas to the west and south of
Philadelphia, including southern New Jersey.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Delaware and Chester Counties have a large, well-educated, and skilled
labor force, with nearly one quarter of the counties&#146; population having earned
a four-year college degree. In addition, Philadelphia&#146;s central location in the
Northeast corridor, infrastructure, and other factors have made the Bank&#146;s
primary market area attractive to many large corporate employers, including
Comcast, Boeing, State Farm Insurance, United Parcel Service, PECO Energy, SAP
America, Inc. and Wawa.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Philadelphia area economy is typical of many large northeastern
cities where the traditional manufacturing-based economy has declined and been
replaced by the service sector, including the health care market.
Crozer/Keystone Health System, Main Line Health, Jefferson Health System, Mercy
Health Corp., and Astra-Zeneca are among the larger health care employers
within the Bank&#146;s market area. According to the Delaware County Chamber of
Commerce, there are more than 65 degree-granting institutions in the Delaware
Valley region, representing a higher density of colleges and universities than
any other area in the United States.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The population of Delaware County is reported at over half a million residents
and is the fifth most populated county in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.
Much of the growth and development continues to be in the western part of the
county and in adjacent Chester County. Chester County&#146;s growth rate is expected
to increase even further in the next decade, and some of the communities in
Chester County that are experiencing the most rapid growth &#151; East Marlborough
Township, New Garden Township and East Goshen &#151; surround the Bank&#146;s Chester
County branch.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We face strong
competition, both in attracting deposits and making real estate and commercial
loans. Our most direct competition for deposits has historically come from
other savings banks, credit unions, and commercial banks located in our market
area. This includes many large regional financial institutions and internet
banks which have even greater financial and marketing resources available to
them. The ability of the Bank to attract and retain core deposits depends on
its ability to provide a competitive rate of return, liquidity, and service
convenience comparable to those offered by competing investment opportunities.
The Bank&#146;s management remains focused on attracting core deposits through its
branch network, business development efforts, and commercial business relationships.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">3<a name="PB_3_072533_5796"></a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Lending
Activities</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">General.</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;
At December&nbsp;31, 2009, the Bank&#146;s total portfolio of loans
receivable amounted to $288.7 million, or 62.2%, of the Bank&#146;s $464.2 million
of total assets at such time.&#160; Prior to
1996 the Bank traditionally concentrated its lending activities on first
mortgage loans secured by residential property.&#160;
However, over the past fourteen years, the Bank has placed an emphasis
on loans secured by commercial real estate properties.&#160; Consistent with such approach, commercial
real estate loans amounted to $131.9 million or 45.7% of the total loan portfolio
at December&nbsp;31, 2009 while single family residential mortgage loans
amounted to $115.0 million or 39.8% of the total loan portfolio.&#160; To a significantly lesser extent, the Bank
also originates multi-family loans, land and construction loans, consumer loans
and commercial business loans.&#160; At December&nbsp;31,
2009, such loan categories amounted to $1.2 million, $24.6 million, $7.6
million and $8.4 million, respectively, or 0.4%, 8.5%, 2.6% and 2.9% of the
total loan portfolio, respectively.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank intends to continue the origination of single-family
residential mortgage loans as well as its emphasis on increasing the
origination of commercial real estate loans.&#160;
For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2009, the Bank&#146;s commercial real
estate loans increased by $8.4 million or 6.8% to $131.9 million. For the year
ended December&nbsp;31, 2009, the Bank&#146;s single-family mortgage loans decreased
by $1.7 million or 1.5% to $115.0 million.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">4<a name="PB_4_072551_2897"></a></font></p>

Maturities</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">.&#160; The following table sets forth the scheduled
contractual maturities of the Bank&#146;s loans receivable at December&nbsp;31,
2009.&#160; Demand loans, loans having no
stated schedule of repayments and no stated maturity and overdraft loans are
reported as due in one year or less.&#160;
Adjustable-rate loans are reported on a contractual basis rather than on
a repricing basis.&#160; The amounts shown for
each period do not take into account loan prepayments and normal amortization
of the Bank&#146;s loan portfolio.</font></p>

<div style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><hr size="1" width="25%" noshade color="black" align="left"></div>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;letter-spacing:0pt;">(1)&nbsp;Does
not include the effects relating to the allowance for loan losses and unearned
income.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;letter-spacing:0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Scheduled contractual amortization of loans does not reflect the
expected term of the Bank&#146;s loan portfolio.&#160;
The average life of loans is substantially less than their contractual
terms because of prepayments and due-on-sale clauses, which gives the Bank the
right to declare a conventional loan immediately due and payable in the event,
among other things, that the borrower sells the real property subject to the
mortgage and the loan is not repaid.&#160; The
average life of mortgage loans tends to increase when current mortgage loan
rates are higher than rates on existing mortgage loans and, conversely,
decrease when rates on existing mortgage loans are lower than current mortgage
loan rates (due to refinancings of adjustable-rate and fixed-rate loans at
lower rates).&#160; Under the latter
circumstance, the weighted average yield on the loan portfolio decreases as
higher-yielding loans are repaid or refinanced at lower rates.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Origination, Purchase and Sale of Loans.</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;
The lending activities of the Bank are subject to the written,
non-discriminatory, underwriting standards and loan origination procedures
established by the Bank&#146;s Board of Directors and management.&#160; Loan originations are obtained by a variety
of sources, including referrals from real estate brokers, builders, existing
customers, advertising, walk-in customers and, to a significant extent,
mortgage brokers who obtain credit reports, appraisals and other documentation
involved with a loan.&#160; Property
valuations are always performed by independent outside appraisers.&#160; Title and hazard insurance are generally
required on all security property other than property securing a home equity
loan, in which case the Bank obtains a title opinion.&#160; The majority of the Bank&#146;s loans are secured
by property located in its primary lending area.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;layout-grid-mode:both;">A commercial residential real estate loan up to
$500,000 must be approved by the loan officer and the Chief Lending </font></p>

of the Senior Loan Committee.&#160; Commercial
real estate loans between $1,000,001 and $2,000,000 must be approved by the
Senior Loan Committee.&#160; Commercial real
estate loans over $2,000,001 must be approved by the Board of Directors.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">A secured
commercial loan up to $250,000 must be approved by the loan officer and the
Chief Lending Officer.&#160; Secured
commercial loans between $250,001 and $500,000 must be approved by the Chief
Executive Officer and one member of the Senior Loan Committee. &#160;Secured commercial loans between $500,001 and
$2,000,000 must be approved by the Senior Loan Committee.&#160; Secured commercial loans over $2,000,001 must
be approved by the Board of Directors.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Unsecured
commercial loans up to $100,000 must be approved by the loan officer and the
Chief Lending Officer.&#160; Unsecured
commercial loans between $100,001 and $500,001 must be approved by the Chief
Executive Officer and one member of the Senior Loan Committee.&#160; Unsecured commercial loans between $500,001
and $750,000 must be approved by the Senior Loan Committee.&#160; Unsecured commercial loans over $750,001 must
be approved by the Board of Directors.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Residential real
estate loans up to $250,000 must be approved by the loan officer and an
Assistant Vice President.&#160; Residential
real estate loans between $205,001 and $500,000 must be approved by the loan
officer and a Senior Vice President.&#160;
Residential real estate loans between $500,001 and $1,000,000 must be
approved by the loan officer and the Chief Lending Officer.&#160; Residential real estate loans between
$1,000,001 and $2,000,000 must be approved by the Senior Loan Committee.&#160; Residential real estate loans over $2,000,001
must be approved by the Board of Directors.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Home equity loans up to $100,000 must be approved by
the loan officer and an Assistant Vice President. Home equity loans between
$100,001 and $250,000 must be approved by the loan officer and a Senior Vice
President. Home equity loans between $250,001 and $750,000 must be approved by
the loan officer and the Chief Lending Officer. Home equity loans between
$750,001 and $2,000,000 must be approved by the Senior Loan Committee. Home
equity loans over $2,000,001 must be approved by the Board of Directors.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Consumer loans up to $100,000 must be approved by the
loan officer and the Chief Lending Officer. Consumer loans between $100,001 and
$2,000,000 must be approved by the Senior Loan Committee. Consumer loans over
$2,000,001 must be approved by the Board of Directors.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank&#146;s
single-family loan originations amounted to $12.2 million and $24.5 million
during 2009 and 2008, respectively.&#160; When
possible, the Bank emphasizes the origination of single-family residential
adjustable-rate mortgage loans (&#147;ARMs&#148;).&#160;
During 2009 and 2008, $3.1 million and $10.3 million single family
residential loans originated had adjustable rates, respectively.&#160; The Bank also originates fixed-rate
single-family residential real estate loans with terms of five, ten, twelve, 15
and 30 years.&#160; Generally, fixed-rate
residential mortgage loans with terms greater than 15 years have been
originated pursuant to commitments to sell such loans to correspondent
mortgage-banking institutions in order to reduce the proportion of the Bank&#146;s
loan portfolio comprised of such assets and reduce interest rate risk.&#160; Loans are sold without any recourse to the
Bank by the purchaser in the event of default on the loan by the borrower and
are sold with servicing released.&#160; The
Bank sold $-0- million and $1.4 million of long-term (generally over 15 years)
fixed-rate residential loans during 2009 and 2008, respectively.&#160; Such loan sales were conducted in furtherance
of the Bank&#146;s asset/liability strategies. At December&nbsp;31, 2009 and December&nbsp;31,
2008, there were no loans held for sale.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In accordance with
the Bank&#146;s increased emphasis on commercial real estate loan originations, such
originations amounted to $37.9 million and $26.9 million during 2009 and 2008,
respectively.&#160; In addition, land and
construction loan originations amounted to $6.7 million and $11.1 million during
2009 and 2008, respectively.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Since 1999, the
Bank has provided single-family residential loan products to borrowers that did
not meet the underwriting criteria of the Federal Home Loan Mortgage
Corporation (&#145;FHLMC&#148;) and the Federal National Mortgage Association (&#147;FNMA&#148;)
and where the borrower&#146;s credit score is below 660.&#160; The Bank recognizes that these loans, which
are considered subprime loans, have additional risk factors as compared to
typical single-family residential lending.&#160;
These loans are generally not saleable in the secondary market due to
the credit risk characteristics of the borrower, the underlying documentation,
the loan-to-value ratio, or the size of the loan, among other factors.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009 and 2008, the Bank&#146;s
single-family loan portfolio included $21.9 million or 19.1% and $24.1 million
or 20.6%, respectively, of such subprime loans.&#160;
The Bank reported $53,000 or 0.1% and $1.9 million or 7.9% of these
loans as non-performing at December&nbsp;31, 2009 and December&nbsp;31, 2008,
respectively.&#160; The Bank recognizes the
additional risk factors associated with subprime lending and utilizes a higher
risk-weighting factor in maintaining its allowance for loan losses with respect
to these loans. In addition, management calculates and reports the delinquency
ratio of its subprime loan portfolio to the Board of Directors on a monthly
basis.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">8<a name="PB_8_075046_7608"></a></font></p>

<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table of Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Historically, the
Bank has not been an active purchaser of loans.&#160;
The Bank purchased $4.0 million and $6.5 million during 2009 and 2008,
respectively, of real estate loans, some of which are located outside of its
primary lending area.&#160; As of December&nbsp;31,
2009, the outstanding balance of such loans included $3.9 million of
residential construction loans and $9.1 million in commercial real estate
loans.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009, none
of these loans were reported as non-performing.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Single-Family
Residential Real Estate Loans</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">.&#160; The Bank has
historically concentrated its lending activities on the origination of loans
secured primarily by first mortgage liens on existing single-family residences
and intends to continue to originate permanent loans secured by first mortgage
liens on single-family residential properties in the future. At December&nbsp;31,
2009, $115.0 million or 39.8% of the Bank&#146;s total loan portfolio consisted of
single-family residential real estate loans.&#160;
Of the $115.0 million of such loans at December&nbsp;31, 2009, $69.2
million or 60.2% had adjustable rates of interest and $45.8 million or 39.8%
had fixed rates of interest.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank&#146;s ARMs typically provide for an interest rate which adjusts
every year after an initial period of three, five, seven or ten years in
accordance with a designated index (the national monthly median cost of funds
or the weekly average yield on U.S. Treasury securities adjusted to a constant
comparable maturity of one year) plus a margin.&#160;
Such loans are typically based on a 30-year amortization schedule.&#160; The amount of any increase or decrease in the
interest rate is presently limited to 200 basis points per year, with a limit
of 600 basis points over the life of the loan.&#160;&#160;&#160; The Bank has not engaged in the practice of
using a cap on the payments that could allow the loan balance to increase
rather than decrease, resulting in negative amortization.&#160; The adjustable-rate loans offered by the
Bank, like many other financial institutions, provide for initial rates of
interest below the rates which would prevail when the index used for repricing
is applied.&#160; However, the Bank
underwrites loans on the basis of the borrower&#146;s ability to pay at the initial
rate which would be in effect without the discount.&#160; Although the Bank continues to emphasize
ARMs, such loan products have not been as attractive due to the lower interest
rate environment which has recently prevailed resulting in a decrease in the
spread between the rates offered on fixed and adjustable rate loans.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Adjustable-rate
loans decrease the risks to the Bank that are associated with changes in
interest rates but involve other risks, primarily because as interest rates
rise, the payment by the borrower rises to the extent permitted by the terms of
the loan, thereby increasing the potential for default.&#160; At the same time, the marketability of the
underlying property may be adversely affected by higher interest rates.&#160; The Bank believes that these risks, which have
not had a material adverse effect on the Bank to date, generally are less than
the risks associated with holding fixed-rate loans in an increasing interest
rate environment.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank has
continued to originate a limited amount of fixed-rate mortgage loans with terms
up to 30 years. The majority of the Bank&#146;s fixed-rate loans with terms of over
15 years are originated pursuant to commitments to sell such loans to
correspondent mortgage banking institutions.&#160;
Fixed-rate loans with terms of 15 years or less are generally originated
for portfolio.&#160; In addition, while the
Bank offers balloon loans with five, seven and ten year terms based on a 20 to
30 year amortization schedule, the Bank has only originated a small amount of
such loans.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank also
offers home equity loans with fixed rates of interest and terms of 15 years or
less.&#160; The Bank does not require that it
hold the first mortgage on the secured property; however, the balance on all
mortgages on the secured property cannot exceed 90% of the value of the secured
property.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009, the
Bank held a first lien on a majority of the properties securing home equity
loans from the Bank.&#160;&#160; At December&nbsp;31,
2009, home equity loans and lines amounted to $21.4 million or 7.4% of the
total loan portfolio, which are included in single family loans.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank is
permitted to lend up to 100% of the appraised value of the real property
securing a residential loan; however, if the amount of a residential loan
originated or refinanced exceeds 90% of the appraised value, the Bank is
required by federal regulations to obtain private mortgage insurance on the
portion of the principal amount that exceeds 80% of the appraised value of the
security property.&#160; Pursuant to
underwriting guidelines adopted by the Board of Directors, the Bank may lend up
to an 80% loan-to-value ratio without private mortgage insurance unless it is
determined that additional collateral in the form of private mortgage insurance
or other acceptable collateral is needed.&#160;
The Bank may lend up to a 90% loan-to-value ratio on a one or two family
owner-occupied residential property as long as additional collateral in the
form of private mortgage insurance or other acceptable collateral enhancements
are obtained. Exceptions to this policy may be made to assist in the Bank&#146;s
community outreach efforts if deemed prudent by the Bank&#146;s Management and with
additional collateral enhancements to reduce the risk inherent in the loan(s).</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Multi-Family
Residential and Commercial Real Estate Loans</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">.&#160; The Bank
originates and, to a lesser extent, purchases mortgage loans for the acquisition
and refinancing of existing multi-family residential and commercial real estate
properties.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009,
$1.2 million or 0.4% of the Bank&#146;s total loan portfolio consisted of loans
secured by existing multi-family residential real estate. &#160;Commercial real estate loans increased from
$123.5 million or 43.8% of the total loan portfolio at December&nbsp;31, 2008
to $131.9 million or 45.7% of the total loan portfolio at December&nbsp;31,
2009. Such increase was due to the Bank&#146;s strategy to increase such
lending.&#160; The Bank intends to </font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">9<a name="PB_9_075057_8146"></a></font></p>

<!-- SEQ.=1,FOLIO='9',FILE='C:\JMS\c900526\09-36066-1\task4002569\36066-1-ba-03.htm',USER='c900526',CD='Mar 19 22:32 2010' -->


<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table of Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">continue to place
an increased emphasis on this type of lending.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The majority of the Bank&#146;s multi-family residential loans are secured
primarily by five to fifteen unit apartment buildings, while the Bank&#146;s
commercial real estate loans are primarily secured by office buildings, hotels,
small retail establishments, restaurants and other facilities.&#160; These types of properties constitute the
majority of the Bank&#146;s commercial real estate loan portfolio.&#160; The majority of the multi-family residential
and commercial real estate loan portfolio at December&nbsp;31, 2009 was secured
by properties located in the Bank&#146;s primary market area.&#160; The five largest loan relationships at December&nbsp;31,
2009 amounted to $6.5 million, $6.3 million, $6.0 million, $5.8 million and
$5.6 million, respectively, all of which were performing in accordance with
their terms and were current at such date.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Multi-family and
commercial real estate loans are made on terms up to 30 years, some of which
include call or balloon provisions ranging from five to 15 years.&#160; The Bank will originate and purchase these
loans either with fixed interest rates or with interest rates which adjust in
accordance with a designated index.&#160; Loan
to value ratios on the Bank&#146;s multi-family and commercial real estate loans are
typically limited to 80% of appraised value at the time the loan is granted.&#160; As part of the criteria for underwriting
multi-family and commercial real estate loans, the Bank generally imposes a
debt coverage ratio (the ratio of net cash from operations before payment of
debt service to debt service) of not less than 1.15.&#160; It is also the Bank&#146;s general policy to
obtain corporate or personal guarantees, as applicable, on its multi-family
residential and commercial real estate loans from the principals of the
borrower.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Multi-family and
commercial real estate lending entails significant additional risks as compared
with single-family residential property lending.&#160; Such loans typically involve large loan
balances to single borrowers or groups of related borrowers.&#160; The payment experience on such loans is
typically dependent on the successful operation of the real estate
project.&#160; The success of such projects is
sensitive to changes in supply and demand conditions in the market for
multi-family and commercial real estate as well as economic conditions
generally.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009,
the Bank had no non-performing multi-family loans and 13 non-performing
commercial real estate loans which amounted to $1.8 million.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Construction
Loans.</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160; The Bank also originates residential and
commercial construction loans, and to a limited degree, land acquisition and
development loans.&#160; Construction loans
are classified as either residential construction loans or commercial real
estate construction loans at the time of origination, depending on the nature
of the property securing the loan.&#160; The
Bank&#146;s construction lending activities generally are limited to the Bank&#146;s
primary market area.&#160; At December&nbsp;31,
2009, construction loans amounted to $24.6 million or 8.5% of the Bank&#146;s total
loan portfolio, which consisted of $12.3 million of residential and $12.3
million of commercial real estate construction loans.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank&#146;s residential construction loans are primarily made to local
real estate builders and developers for the purpose of constructing
single-family homes and single-family residential developments.&#160; Upon successful application, credit review
and analysis of personal and corporate financial statements, the Bank will
grant local builders lines of credit up to designated amounts.&#160; These loans may be used for the purpose of
constructing model homes, including a limited number for inventory.&#160; In some instances, lines of credit will also
be granted for purposes of acquiring improved lots or the purchase of
construction in process and developing of speculative properties thereon.&#160; Once approved for a construction loan or
credit line, a developer submits a progress report and a request for
payment.&#160; Generally, the Bank makes
payments under the stage of completion method.&#160;
Prior to making payment, the Bank inspects all construction sites and
verifies that the work being submitted for payments has been performed.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank&#146;s
commercial construction loans are generally made to local developers and others
for the purpose of developing commercial real estate properties such as small
office buildings and hotels, storage facilities and commercial building
renovations.&#160; The application, credit
review and disbursement process are similar to those mentioned above for the
Bank&#146;s residential construction loans.&#160;&#160;
The five largest real estate construction loans had outstanding balances
of $6.0 million, $3.7 million, $2.9 million, $2.0 million, and $1.7 million as
of December&nbsp;31, 2009.&#160; The $6.0
million loan is a land and development loan for a mixed use commercial real
estate project located in Bradenton, Florida, and was classified as special
mention at December&nbsp;31, 2009.&#160; The
$3.7 million loan was restructured in December&nbsp;of 2009, which management
considers to be a troubled debt restructuring, and was classified as
non-performing as of December&nbsp;31, 2009.&#160;
The $2.9 million and $1.7 million loans are residential construction
projects located in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania and are both classified as
special mention due to slower than anticipated sales.&#160; The $2.0 million loan is a performing
commercial construction loan in Philadelphia..</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank&#146;s
construction loans generally have maturities of 12 to 36 months, with payments
being made monthly on an interest-only basis.&#160;
These interest payments are generally paid out of an interest reserve,
which is established in connection with the origination of the loan.&#160; Generally, such loans adjust monthly based on
the prime rate plus a margin of up to 2.0%. Residential and commercial real
estate construction loans are generally made with maximum loan to value ratios
of 80% and 75%, respectively, on an as completed basis.&#160; The Bank utilizes interest rate floors on all
commercial loans and lines of credit whenever possible.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">10<a name="PB_10_075107_7091"></a></font></p>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table of Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Construction
lending is generally considered to involve a higher level of risk as compared
to single-family residential lending, due to the concentration of principal in
a limited number of loans and borrowers and the effects of general economic
conditions on developers and builders.&#160;
Moreover, a construction loan can involve additional risks because of
the inherent difficulty in estimating both a property&#146;s value at completion of
the project and the estimated cost (including interest) of the project.&#160; The nature of these loans is such that they
are generally more difficult to evaluate and monitor. In addition, speculative
construction loans to a builder are not necessarily pre-sold and thus pose a
greater potential risk to the Bank than construction loans to individuals on
their personal residences.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank has
attempted to minimize the foregoing risks by, among other things, limiting the
number of units built to two or three sample units plus any under agreement of
sale and limiting the extent of its construction lending and has adopted
underwriting guidelines which impose stringent loan-to-value, debt service and
other requirements for loans which are believed to involve higher elements of
credit risk, by limiting the geographic area in which the Bank will do business
and by working with builders with whom it has established relationships.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009, the Bank had one
non-performing construction loan which had an outstanding balance of $3.7
million.&#160; In December&nbsp;2009, this
loan was restructured and management considers this a troubled debt
restructuring.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Consumer
Loans</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">.&#160; The Bank offers consumer loans in order to
provide a full range of financial services to its customers and because such
loans generally have shorter terms and higher interest rates than mortgage
loans.&#160; The consumer loans presently
offered by the Bank include student loans, deposit account secured loans and
lines of credit.&#160; Consumer loans amounted
to $7.6 million or 2.6% of the total loan portfolio at December&nbsp;31,
2009.&#160; Student loans amounted to $7.1
million or 2.5% of the total loan portfolio at December&nbsp;31, 2009.&#160; Such loans are made to local students for a
term of ten years, presently with adjustable interest rates.&#160; The interest rate is determined by the U.S.
Department of Education.&#160; Loan repayment
obligations do not begin until the student has completed his or her
education.&#160; The principal and interest on
such loans is guaranteed by the U.S. Government.&#160; Loans secured by deposit accounts amounted to
$482,000 or 0.2% of the total loan portfolio at December&nbsp;31, 2009.&#160; Such loans are originated for up to 90% of
the account balance, with a hold placed on the account restricting the
withdrawal of the account balance.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Consumer loans
generally have shorter terms and higher interest rates than mortgage loans but
generally involve more credit risk than mortgage loans because of the type and
nature of the collateral and, in certain cases, the absence of collateral.&#160; In addition, consumer lending collections are
dependent on the borrower&#146;s continuing financial stability, and thus are more
likely to be adversely effected by job loss, divorce, illness and personal
bankruptcy.&#160; In most cases, any
repossessed collateral for a defaulted consumer loan will not provide an
adequate source of repayment of the outstanding loan balance because of
improper repair and maintenance of the underlying collateral.&#160; The remaining deficiency often does not
warrant further substantial collection efforts against the borrower.&#160; The Bank believes that the generally higher
yields earned on consumer loans compensate for the increased credit risk
associated with such loans and that consumer loans are important to its efforts
to provide a full range of services to its customers.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009, there were 60
non-performing student loans which amounted to $153,000, compared to 22
non-performing student loans which amounted to $75,000 at December&nbsp;31,
2008.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Commercial
Business Loans.</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160; In September&nbsp;1997, the Bank opened a
commercial loan department to provide a full range of commercial loan products
to small business customers in its primary marketing area.&#160; These loans generally have shorter terms and
higher interest rates as compared to mortgage loans.&#160; Such loans amounted to $8.5 million or 2.9%
of the total loan portfolio at December&nbsp;31, 2009 and were primarily
secured by inventories and other business assets.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Although
commercial business loans generally are considered to involve greater credit
risk than other certain types of loans, management intends to continue to offer
commercial business loans to small businesses located in its primary market
area.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009, the
Bank had 4 non-performing commercial business loans which amounted $472,000.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Loan Fee
Income</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">.&#160; In addition to interest earned on loans, the
Bank receives income from fees in connection with loan originations, loan
modifications, late payments, prepayments and for miscellaneous services
related to its loans.&#160; Income from these
activities varies from period to period with the volume and type of loans made
and competitive conditions. The Bank charges loan origination fees which are
calculated as a percentage of the amount borrowed.&#160; Loan origination and commitment fees and all
incremental direct loan origination costs are deferred and recognized over the
contractual remaining lives of the related loans on a level yield basis.&#160; Discounts and premiums on loans purchased are
amortized in the same manner.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">11<a name="PB_11_075508_4141"></a></font></p>

<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table
of Contents</a></font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Asset
Quality</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Loans are placed
on non-accrual status when, in the judgment of management, the probability of
collection of interest is deemed to be insufficient to warrant further
accrual.&#160; When a loan is placed on
non-accrual status, previously accrued but unpaid interest is deducted from
interest income.&#160; The Bank does not
accrue interest on real estate loans past due 90 days or more unless, in the
opinion of management, the value of the property securing the loan exceeds the
outstanding balance of the loan (principal, interest and escrows) and
collection is probable.&#160; The Bank
provides an allowance for accrued interest deemed uncollectible.&#160; Such allowance amounted to approximately
$138,000 at December&nbsp;31, 2009 compared to $492,000 at December&nbsp;31,
2008. Accrued interest receivable is reported net of the allowance for
uncollected interest.&#160; Loans may be
reinstated to accrual status when all payments are brought current and, in the
opinion of management, collection of the remaining balance can be reasonably
expected.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Real estate
acquired by the Bank as a result of foreclosure or by deed-in-lieu of
foreclosure is classified as other real estate owned (OREO) until sold and is
initially recorded at the fair value at the date of acquisition.&#160;&#160; After the date of acquisition, all costs
incurred in maintaining the property are expensed and costs incurred for the
improvement or development of such property are capitalized up to the extent of
their fair value.&#160; As of December&nbsp;31,
2009, the Bank had approximately $3.0 million in OREO.&#160; The $3.0 million consists of one commercial
property in the amount of $651,000, three improved building lots totaling
$930,000, one unimproved lot in the amount of $38,000, and four single family
residences totaling $1.4 million.&#160; All of
the properties are located within the Banks market area except one of the
single family residences which is located in Tampa, Florida with a carrying
value of $49,000.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Under accounting
principles generally accepted in the United States of America (&#147;GAAP&#148;), the
Bank is required to account for certain loan modifications or restructurings as
&#147;troubled debt restructurings.&#148;&#160; In
general, the modification or restructuring of a debt constitutes a troubled
debt restructuring if the Bank, for economic or legal reasons related to the
borrower&#146;s financial difficulties, grants a concession to the borrower that the
Bank would not otherwise consider.&#160; Debt
restructurings or loan modifications for a borrower do not necessarily always
constitute troubled debt restructurings, however, and troubled debt
restructurings do not necessarily result in non-accrual loans.&#160; The Bank did not have any troubled debt
restructurings as of December&nbsp;31, 2008. At December&nbsp;31, 2009, the
Bank had one troubled debt restructuring construction loan which had an
outstanding balance of $3.7 million.&#160;
Management decided to place the loan on non-accrual until the borrower
shows the ability to pay in accordance with the restructured terms.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Delinquent
Loans</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">.&#160; The following table sets forth information
concerning delinquent loans at December&nbsp;31, 2009, in dollar amounts and as
a percentage of each category of the Bank&#146;s loan portfolio.&#160; The amounts presented represent the total
outstanding principal balances of the related loans, rather than the actual
payment amounts which are past due.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">If the Bank&#146;s $6.5 million of non-accruing loans at December&nbsp;31,
2009 had been current in accordance with their terms during 2009, the gross
income on such loans would have been approximately $335,000 for 2009.&#160; The Bank actually recorded $136,000 in
interest income on such loans for 2009.&#160;
If the Bank&#146;s $5.2 million of non-accruing loans at December&nbsp;31,
2008 had been current in accordance with their terms during 2008, the gross
income on such loans would have been approximately $347,000 for 2008.&#160; The Bank actually recorded $121,000 in
interest income on such loans for 2008.&#160;
Loans are placed on non-accrual when interest past due exceeds 90 days,
unless the loan is well secured and in the process of collection.</font></p>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table of Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank&#146;s nonperforming assets, which consist of nonaccruing loans,
accruing loans 90 days or more delinquent and other real estate owned (which
includes real estate acquired through, or in lieu of, foreclosure) increased to
$10.8 million or 2.33% of total assets at December&nbsp;31, 2009 from $7.0
million or 1.65% of total assets at December&nbsp;31, 2008.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009, the Bank&#146;s $10.8
million of nonperforming assets consisted of $1.4 million of accruing loans 90
days or more delinquent, $6.4 million of nonaccrual loans and $3.0 million in
other real estate owned. At December&nbsp;31, 2009, nonperforming loans
consisted of $1.7 million in single-family residential real estate loans, $1.8
million in commercial real estate loans, $3.7 million in a residential real
estate construction loan, $472,000 in commercial business loans, and $153,000
in consumer and other loans.&#160; The $1.8
million of nonperforming commercial real estate loans consists of 13 loans to 7
borrowers that are the result of cash flow stress primarily due to the current
economic conditions.&#160; The Bank&#146;s
management continues to aggressively pursue the collection and resolution of
all delinquent loans.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;page-break-after:avoid;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Classified
Assets.</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160; Federal regulations require that each insured
savings association classify its assets on a regular basis. In addition, in
connection with examinations of insured institutions, federal examiners have
authority to identify problem assets and, if appropriate, classify them.&#160; There are three regulatory classifications
for problem assets: &#147;substandard,&#148; &#147;doubtful&#148; and &#147;loss.&#148;&#160; Substandard assets have one or more defined
weaknesses and are characterized by the distinct possibility that the insured
institution will sustain some loss if the deficiencies are not corrected.&#160; Doubtful assets have the weaknesses of
substandard assets with the additional characteristic that the weaknesses
make&nbsp;collection or liquidation in full on the basis of currently existing
facts, conditions and values questionable, and there is a high possibility of
loss.&#160; An asset classified loss is
considered uncollectible and of such little value that continuance as an asset
of the institution is not warranted.&#160;
Another category designated &#147;special mention&#148; also must be established
and maintained for assets which have a weakness but do not currently expose an
insured institution to a sufficient degree of risk to warrant classification as
substandard, doubtful or loss.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;page-break-after:avoid;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">At December&nbsp;31, 2009, the Bank had $20.3 million of classified
assets, of which $12.6 million consisted of loans classified as special
mention, $7.7 million consisted of loans classified as substandard, and no
loans classified as doubtful.&#160; The $12.6
million of loans classified as special mention consisted of $787,000 in
commercial real estate loans and $11.8 million in real estate construction
loans.&#160; The $11.8 million includes four
residential real estate construction loans to three borrowers amounting to $4.2
million and two commercial real estate construction loans amounting to $7.6
million at December&nbsp;31, 2009.&#160; All
of these loans are located in the Bank&#146;s primary market except for one mixed
use commercial real estate project located in Bradenton, Florida, which have
been classified as special mention primarily due to slower than anticipated
sales.&#160; The $7.7 million of loans
designated as substandard consisted of $1.7 million of single-family real
estate loans, $1.5 million in commercial real estate loans, $3.7 million in
construction real estate, and $472,000 in commercial business loans.&#160; The $3.7 million real estate construction
loan represents 16 remaining substantially completed residential condominium
units located in center city Philadelphia and was restructured in December of
2009,&#160; which management considers to be a
troubled debt restructuring.&#160; The Company
does not knowingly lend to subprime borrowers, except as disclosed in
&#147;Origination, Purchase and Sale of Loans&#148;, and has not been materially directly
impacted by the current subprime crisis as of December 31, 2009.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Allowance for Loan Losses</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">.&#160;
The allowance for loan losses is increased by charges to income and
decreased by chargeoffs (net of recoveries).&#160;
Allowances are provided for specific loans when losses are probable and
can be estimated.&#160; When this occurs, management
considers the remaining principal balance, fair value and estimated net
realizable value of the property collateralizing the loan.&#160; Current and future operating and/or sales
conditions are also considered.&#160; These
estimates are susceptible to changes that could result in material adjustments
to results of operations.&#160; Recovery of
the carrying value of such loans is dependent to a great extent on economic,
operating and other conditions that may be beyond management&#146;s control.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">General loan loss
reserves are established as an allowance for losses based on inherent probable
risk of loss in the loan portfolio.&#160; In
assessing risk, management considers historical experience, volume and
composition of lending conducted by the Bank, industry standards, status of
non-performing loans, general economic conditions as they relate to the market
area and other factors related to the collectibility of the Bank&#146;s loan
portfolio.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Impaired loans are
predominantly measured based on the fair value of the collateral.&#160; The provision for loan losses charged to
expense is based upon past loan loss experience and an evaluation of probable
losses and impairment existing in the current loan portfolio.&#160; A loan is considered to be impaired when,
based upon current information and events, it is probable that the Bank will be
unable to collect all amounts due according to the original contractual terms
of the loan.&#160; An insignificant delay or
insignificant shortfall in amounts of payments does not necessarily result in
the loan being identified as impaired.&#160;
For this purpose, delays less than 90 days are considered to be
insignificant.&#160; Large groups of smaller
balance homogeneous loans, including residential real estate and consumer
loans, are collectively evaluated for impairment, except for loans restructured
under a troubled debt restructuring.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Although management uses
the best information available to make determinations with respect to the
provisions for loan losses, additional provisions for loan losses may be
required to be established in the future should economic or other conditions
change substantially.&#160; In addition, the
Pennsylvania Department of Banking and the FDIC, as an integral part of their
examination process, periodically review the Bank&#146;s allowance for loan
losses.&#160; Such agencies may require the
Bank to recognize additions to such allowance based on their judgments about
information available to them at the time of their examination.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table of Contents</a></font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Investment
Activities</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Mortgage-Backed
Securities.</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160; Mortgage-backed securities (which also are
known as mortgage participation certificates or pass-through certificates)
represent a participation interest in a pool of single-family or multi-family
mortgages, the principal and interest payments on which are passed from the
mortgage originators, through intermediaries (generally U.S. Government
agencies and government sponsored enterprises) that pool and repackage the
participation interests in the form of securities, to investors such as the
Bank.&#160; Such U.S. Government agencies and
government sponsored enterprises, which guarantee the payment of principal and
interest to investors, primarily include the FHLMC, the FNMA and the Government
National Mortgage Association (&#147;GNMA&#148;).</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-variant:normal !important;letter-spacing:0pt;">The FHLMC is a public corporation chartered by the U.S.
Government.&#160; The FHLMC issues
participation certificates backed principally by conventional mortgage
loans.&#160; The FHLMC guarantees the timely
payment of interest and the ultimate return of principal within one year.&#160; The FNMA is a private corporation chartered
by the U.S. Congress with a mandate to establish a secondary market for
conventional mortgage loans.&#160; The FNMA
guarantees the timely payment of principal and interest on FNMA
securities.&#160; FHLMC and FNMA securities
are not backed by the full faith and credit of the United States, but because
the FHLMC and the FNMA are U.S. Government sponsored enterprises, these
securities are considered high quality investments with minimal credit
risks.&#160; The GNMA is a government agency
within the Department of Housing and Urban Development which is intended to help
finance government assisted housing programs.&#160;
GNMA securities are backed by FHA-insured and VA-guaranteed loans, and
the timely payment of principal and interest on GNMA securities are guaranteed
by the GNMA and backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S.
Government.&#160; Because the FHLMC, the FNMA
and the GNMA were established to provide support for low- and middle-income
housing, there are limits to the maximum size of loans that qualify for these
programs.&#160; For example, the FNMA and the
FHLMC currently limit their loans secured by a single-family, owner-occupied
residence to $417,000.&#160; To accommodate
larger-sized loans, and loans that, for other reasons, do not conform to the
agency programs, a number of private institutions have established their own
home-loan origination and securitization programs.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;letter-spacing:0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Mortgage-backed
securities typically are issued with stated principal amounts, and the
securities are backed by pools of mortgages that have loans with interest rates
that are within a range and have varying maturities.&#160; The cash flow associated with the underlying
pool of mortgages, i.e., fixed rate or adjustable rate, as well as prepayment
risk, are passed on to the certificate holder.&#160;
The life of a mortgage-backed pass-through security thus approximates
the life of the underlying mortgages.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The following
table sets forth the fair value of the Bank&#146;s mortgage-backed securities
portfolio designated as available for sale at the dates indicated.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

  </td>
  <td width="2%" valign="bottom" style="padding:0in 0in 0in 0in;width:2.22%;">
  <p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><b><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:1.0pt;font-weight:bold;">&nbsp;</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Mortgage-backed
securities generally increase the quality of the Bank&#146;s assets by virtue of the
insurance or guarantees that back them, they are more liquid than individual
mortgage loans and may be used to collateralize borrowings or other obligations
of the Bank.&#160; At December 31, 2009, $3.1
million of the Bank&#146;s mortgage-backed securities were pledged to secure various
obligations of the Bank.&#160; See Note 4 to
the Consolidated Financial Statements in Item 8.&#160; The Company does not knowingly invest in
subprime financial instruments, and has not been materially impacted by the
current subprime crisis as of December 31, 2009.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Information
regarding the contractual maturities and weighted average yield of the Bank&#146;s
mortgage-backed securities portfolio at December&nbsp;31, 2009 is presented
below.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">(1)&nbsp;All
mortgage-backed securities are designated as available for sale.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The actual
maturity of a mortgage-backed security is typically less than its stated
maturity due to prepayments of the underlying mortgages.&#160; Prepayments that are faster than anticipated
may shorten the life of the security and increase or decrease its yield to
maturity if the security was purchased at a discount or premium,
respectively.&#160; The yield is based upon
the interest income and the amortization of any premium or discount related to
the mortgage-backed security.&#160; In
accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States
of America, premiums and discounts are amortized over the estimated lives of
the loans, which decrease and increase interest income, respectively.&#160; The prepayment assumptions used to determine
the amortization period for premiums and discounts can significantly affect the
yield of the mortgage-backed security, when premiums or discounts are involved,
and these assumptions are reviewed periodically to reflect actual
prepayments.&#160; Although prepayments of
underlying mortgages depend on many factors, including the type of mortgages,
the coupon rate, the age of mortgages, the geographical location of the
underlying real estate collateralizing the mortgages and general levels of
market interest rates, the difference between the interest rates on the
underlying mortgages and the prevailing mortgage interest rates generally is
the most significant determinant of the rate of prepayments.&#160; During periods of falling mortgage interest
rates, if the coupon rate of the underlying mortgages exceeds the prevailing
market interest rates offered for mortgage loans, refinancing </font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">18<a name="PB_18_083242_5796"></a></font></p>

<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table of Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">generally
increases and accelerates the prepayment of the underlying mortgages and the
related security.&#160; Under such
circumstances, the Bank may be subject to reinvestment risk because to the
extent that the Bank&#146;s mortgage-backed securities amortize or prepay faster
than anticipated, the Bank may not be able to reinvest the proceeds of such
repayments and prepayments at a comparable rate.&#160; During periods of rising interest rates,
prepayment of the underlying mortgages generally slow down when the coupon rate
of such mortgages is less than the prevailing market rate.&#160; The Bank may be subject to extension risk
when this occurs.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Investment
Securities.</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160; The investment policy of the Bank, as
established by the Board of Directors, is designed primarily to provide and
maintain liquidity and to generate a favorable return on investments without
incurring undue interest rate risk, credit risk, and investment portfolio asset
concentrations.&#160; The Bank&#146;s investment
policy takes into account the Bank&#146;s business plan, interest rate management,
the current economic environment, the types of securities to be held and other
safety and soundness considerations.&#160; The
Bank&#146;s investment policy is currently implemented by the Chief Executive
Officer and reviewed and evaluated by the Asset Liability Committee.&#160; The Asset Liability Committee is required to
issue a written compliance report to the Board of Directors at least quarterly.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank is authorized to
invest in obligations issued or fully guaranteed by the U.S. Government,
certain federal agency obligations, insured municipal obligations, certain
mutual funds, investment grade corporate debt securities and other specified
investments.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009,
the Bank&#146;s investment securities amounted to $52.3 million, of which $28.9
million was designated as available for sale and $23.4 million was designated
as held to maturity.&#160; The Bank has
designated the majority of its investment securities as available for sale in
order to respond to changes in market rates, increases in loan demand, and
changes in liquidity needs.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

table sets forth certain information relating to the Bank&#146;s investment
securities portfolio at the dates indicated.</font></p>

  spread differential is primarily due to the general lack of investor interest
